title: Best Open Source BI Tools in 2026: nao, Metabase, Lightdash
summary: nao, Metabase, Lightdash, Superset, Evidence, Streamlit and Redash compared on license, self-hosting, AI features and dbt support, with the limits of each.
body_markdown:
Picking an open source BI tool used to be a question of charts and licenses. In 2026, almost every tool on this list also ships an AI feature, and the questions change: who will ask the questions, in which interface, and where do your metric definitions live?


This guide compares seven open source tools: **nao, Metabase, Lightdash, Apache Superset, Evidence, Streamlit and Redash** . For each one: what it does well, what its AI features actually include, and where it falls short. We build nao, so read section 1 with that in mind: its limits are listed like everyone else's. Facts about the other tools come from their own docs and repos, as of November 2026.


## Why open source BI is back on the table


Two things changed this year.


First, the dashboard is no longer the only interface. A dashboard needs someone to anticipate the question, and more and more reporting happens on demand, in a chat ([a LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/000matthewwilliams7795_i-expect-a-lot-less-business-reporting-to-activity-7529626617799680000-H9td) made the same point this month). That only works with consistent definitions and a clean schema, and no tool does that work for you.


Second, the bottleneck moved below the BI tool. A team[posted on r/PostgreSQL](https://www.reddit.com/r/PostgreSQL/comments/1y1ilvb/multitenant_dashboards_with_postgres_rls_started/) that their Metabase and Superset dashboards slowed to 14-second scans once their events table crossed 42M rows with row-level security. Swapping BI tools would not have helped; putting Cube Core, an open source semantic layer, in front of Postgres dropped p95 dashboard waits to under 60ms.


Another team[moving off free Looker Studio](https://www.reddit.com/r/businessanalyst/comments/1y1itpd/what_broke_when_looking_for_looker_studio/) ended up with 18 report copies and marketing and finance using different revenue filters. After testing Preset (managed Superset) and Evidence, they still had to move metrics into versioned YAML.


The lesson from both threads: pick your BI tool for the interface, and own your **definitions** somewhere you control. We reached the same conclusion in our[benchmark of 20 AI data agents](https://getnao.io/blog/ai-data-agents-compared/) .

GitHub stars as of November 2026: Superset 75.7k, Metabase 50.6k, Streamlit 46.5k, Redash 28.9k, Evidence 7.1k, Lightdash 6.3k, nao 2k.


## 1. nao: open source agentic BI


**[getnao.io](https://getnao.io/) ·[github.com/getnao/nao](https://github.com/getnao/nao)**


nao is an open source analytics agent your data team builds and controls, on any warehouse: BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Postgres, Redshift, ClickHouse, DuckDB and more. Business users ask in plain English and get the SQL, the chart and the answer, in the nao app,[Slack](https://getnao.io/blog/setup-ai-analytics-slack-bot-open-source/) , Teams, or Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor through the[nao MCP app](https://getnao.io/blog/launching-nao-mcp-app/) .


**Dashboards come from a question.** Ask "Build a dashboard of revenue by country" and the agent writes the SQL, runs it on your warehouse and builds a[story](https://getnao.io/blog/how-to-turn-chat-with-data-into-shareable-stories/) : KPIs, charts, tabs, and filters. **Live stories** refresh on a schedule, every save is versioned, and you can edit a chart directly instead of re-prompting.


**Custom stories** turn the same data into interactive data apps and slide decks in your own brand, and[automations](https://getnao.io/blog/launching-nao-automations/) replace dashboard subscriptions: "Every Monday, email me the weekly business review", or "Check daily if revenue dropped more than 10%, only notify me if it did".


**The answers rest on a context layer you own.** nao syncs your warehouse metadata, your dbt repo, your docs and your rules into files in a git repository. You can wire in a semantic layer like dbt MetricFlow when tests show you need one. Then[nao test](https://getnao.io/blog/analytics-agent-benchmark-context-stack/) runs your key questions against the SQL you expect, so you know the score before business users see the agent.


If you are leaving a BI tool, nao has[migration skills for Metabase and Tableau](https://docs.getnao.io/nao-agent/chat/bi/migrate-bi) : a Metabase dashboard becomes a nao story, a saved question becomes a chart, and anything that can't carry over is reported.


**Limits:** nao is the youngest project on this list (2k GitHub stars), so its community, examples and integrations are smaller. The agent is only as good as the context your data team writes: plan time for rules, docs and tests before rolling it out to business users. And you pay your own LLM usage.


**Best for:** data teams that want business users to get answers and dashboards from an agent, with the context and the tests in their own repo.


## 2. Metabase: easiest for business users


**[metabase.com](https://www.metabase.com/) ·[github.com/metabase/metabase](https://github.com/metabase/metabase)**


Metabase is the open source BI tool most teams try first: a visual query builder, a full SQL editor, interactive dashboards, alerts, and SDKs to embed charts in your product, on 20+ databases and warehouses.


The AI side moved fast. **Metabot** creates charts from natural language, writes and fixes SQL, and finds content, and Metabase AI now also includes an MCP server and a CLI. According to the[Metabot docs](https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/ai/metabot) , it is available on every plan. On self-hosted open source, you connect your own AI provider: the Metabase AI service itself is Cloud only. Verified content for Metabot and AI usage auditing are Pro and Enterprise features.


**Limits:** in our own test, setup was easy and the UI fast, but the agent had no access to our dbt docs, missed a churn column and answered wrong. Its context is what lives inside Metabase (glossary, segments, measures), so reliability means pushing your definitions into Metabase. Full notes on our[nao vs Metabase page](https://getnao.io/resources/compare/metabase/) .


**Best for:** teams where business users browse and tweak existing questions.


## 3. Lightdash: built for dbt teams


**[lightdash.com](https://www.lightdash.com/) ·[github.com/lightdash/lightdash](https://github.com/lightdash/lightdash)**


Lightdash reads your dbt project (dbt Core, dbt Cloud) or its own Lightdash YAML, so metrics are defined once in code. The core is MIT and free to self-host.


Its **AI agents** answer questions on your semantic layer, use knowledge documents and skills, run in Slack or embedded in your app, and come with evaluation suites built from real threads. An MCP server serves Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor.


**Limits:** on the[pricing page](https://www.lightdash.com/pricing) , AI agents and MCP are listed on Cloud Pro and Enterprise (usage-based), not in the self-hosted open source tier. And the agent answers within the semantic layer: questions outside the metrics you defined need SQL.


**Best for:** teams already on dbt who want governed metrics and are fine with the agent on Lightdash Cloud.


## 4. Apache Superset: most flexible


**[superset.apache.org](https://superset.apache.org/) ·[github.com/apache/superset](https://github.com/apache/superset)**


Superset is the Apache-licensed heavyweight. It ships a no-code chart builder, **SQL Lab** (a web SQL IDE with Jinja templating), a lightweight semantic layer for custom dimensions and metrics, 40+ visualizations and a caching layer. It queries nearly any SQL database with a Python DB-API driver and a SQLAlchemy dialect.


There is no chat UI in the README, but the codebase now includes an **MCP service** : you connect Claude Desktop or another agent to your Superset instance, and it can query data, create charts and manage dashboards.


**Limits:** Superset is a platform to run, and as the Looker Studio thread shows, analysts tweaking chart SQL can still make definitions drift. The AI part is bring-your-own-agent: nothing tests whether its answers are right.


**Best for:** data teams that want a free, extensible alternative to proprietary BI and have the engineers to run it.


## 5. Evidence: BI as code


**[github.com/evidence-dev/evidence](https://github.com/evidence-dev/evidence)**


Evidence is "business intelligence as code": reports written in SQL and Markdown, built into a static site you self-host or publish on Evidence Studio. You can write them with Evidence's agent, Claude Code or Cursor.


The Looker Studio team liked it: version control was fixed and scheduled static builds stopped runaway BigQuery costs.


**Limits:** the same team found that self-serve slicing and natural-language follow-ups sent people back to Google Sheets. Reports are built by people who write SQL; business users read them.


**Best for:** analysts who want reports as code, reviewed in pull requests.


## 6. Streamlit: data apps in Python


**[streamlit.io](https://streamlit.io/) ·[github.com/streamlit/streamlit](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit)**


Streamlit is an Apache 2.0 Python framework for data apps and dashboards: each app is a Python script, written by you or your coding agent, with no separate frontend. It handles the interface, state, caching, sign-in (` st.login` ) and theming. You run it in your own cloud, on the free Community Cloud, or inside Snowflake, which owns Streamlit.


On AI, Streamlit gives you building blocks rather than an agent: chat elements (` st.chat_input` ,` st.write_stream` ) to build your own chat app over your data, and, according to its README, every app can be used as a tool by Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client.


**Limits:** every dashboard is code someone writes and maintains, so business users depend on Python developers for changes. There is no semantic layer or dbt integration built in, and a chat app you build yourself comes with no way to measure whether its answers are right.


**Best for:** Python teams that need custom data apps (forecasts, what-if simulators, review queues) more than a self-serve BI tool.


## 7. Redash: SQL-first and simple


**[github.com/getredash/redash](https://github.com/getredash/redash)**


Redash is a browser-based query editor with a schema browser and autocomplete, drag-and-drop visualizations, dashboards, scheduled refreshes, alerts and a REST API. It supports more than 35 SQL and NoSQL sources and is BSD-licensed.


**Limits:** the README describes no AI features, and there is no semantic layer: every chart is a SQL query.


**Best for:** SQL users who want to share queries and simple dashboards.

## How to choose an open source BI tool


### First: keep your BI, add an agent, or migrate?


- **Your current BI tool's AI features cover the need** : invest in them (Metabot on Metabase, AI agents on Lightdash).
- **Your current BI is fine for reporting, not for questions** : keep it for reporting and add an AI agent next to it. nao connects to the warehouse, not to the BI tool, so it runs alongside any of the tools above.
- **Neither** : migrate to an AI-native tool, and plan the migration cost. nao's migration skills move Metabase and Tableau dashboards into stories and report what can't carry over.


### Then: what is your main priority?


Main priority What to look for In this list


UI for data users SQL, notebooks or code Superset, Redash, Evidence, Streamlit, nao (SQL shown with every answer, context as code)


UI for business users Drag and drop, chat Metabase, nao


Security Self-hosted, including the AI agent nao, Metabase (with your own AI key)


No extra tool The AI features of the tool you already run Metabase, Lightdash


Reliability Evaluation and visibility on what the agent answers nao (` nao test` ), Lightdash (evaluation suites)


Best price Open source, you only pay for LLM usage nao, Metabase with your own AI key


Fewer dashboard tickets Business users build and change dashboards themselves nao (stories from a question), Metabase (point and click)


Answers where people work Slack, Teams, Claude, ChatGPT nao, Metabase (Slack), Lightdash (Slack)


Mature community Years of production use, many plugins and answers online Superset, Metabase, Streamlit


### Finally: two questions about your team


**Who builds the charts?** Business users clicking around: Metabase. Business users who would rather ask than click: nao. Analysts writing SQL: Superset or Redash, or nao if you want the agent to write the first draft and show its SQL. Analysts writing code in git: Evidence. Python developers building apps: Streamlit. Anyone asking questions in plain English, in Slack or a chat app: nao.


**Where do your metric definitions live?** In dbt: Lightdash reads them natively, and nao syncs your dbt repo as agent context. In a dbt MetricFlow semantic layer: nao queries it natively. In docs, a wiki or people's heads: nao reads docs and a rules file, so you can write them down without a semantic layer first. If they live in five dashboards, fix that first. Both Reddit threads above ended with definitions moved into code, not with a new BI tool.


Whatever you pick, test the agent on 20-40 real questions before rolling it out. That is how we took our own agent[from 45% to 86% reliability](https://getnao.io/blog/improve-analytics-agent-reliability-steps/) .
